prize_parts.citation: For the development of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that entrap nucleic acids and release them inside cells, enabling nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: I keep B060 with Cullis, Hope and Madden as my preferred single-part prize. The chemical content is a set of physical-chemical design rules for a self-assembled system: an ionizable lipid is cationic at low pH, where it entraps polyanionic nucleic acid during formulation, and close to neutral at physiological pH, so the particle is tolerated in circulation. Acidification in the endosome re-charges the lipid and favours non-bilayer phase behaviour that drives release into the cytosol. These rules were established and then reproduced by independent academic and industrial groups. They underlie the first approved siRNA drug and the mRNA vaccines, so the evidence is mature and clinical at very large scale. Hearing the round-1 exchange, I have dropped B007 as an alternative, since Aili, Brzezinski and Linke all said convincingly that the in vivo status of condensates is unsettled and credit among five names is unresolved. My preferred configuration is unchanged, but I now regard it as one of several defensible choices, not the obvious one. The round-1 files show no majority, and the chair's point stands that B014 and B046 trade novelty against credit clarity. I judge B060 to sit between them: its scientific principle is more physical-chemical than B046's extension of a known catalytic cycle and its clinical proof is far stronger than B014's, but its credit problem is real and I do not hide it.
statement.case_against: Credit is the central weakness. The Vancouver trio is my best reading of who established ionizable-lipid entrapment and pH-triggered release, but Anderson and Langer (lipidoid screening) and MacLachlan (lipid optimisation for siRNA delivery) made contributions that later products rely on, and a three-name cap leaves them out. Patent disputes mean the published record may not settle priority, and I am recalling the early papers from memory rather than checking them. A formulation is also less molecularly defined than a catalytic cycle or a degrader, so some colleagues will say that this is engineering optimisation rather than a distinct chemical discovery. The 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside-modified mRNA does not honour the delivery chemistry, but it does make the Committee's wording about what is new in chemistry more delicate. Finally, I am a lipid physical chemist and may overrate how much the phase-behaviour story explains.

responses.point: Aili puts B014 first with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, argues that the cereblon mechanism ties the PROTAC concept to clinically proven thalidomide-class drugs, and names B060 as the first fallback if the Committee judges degraders to be early.
responses.response: The cereblon link is the best answer I have heard to the clinical-validation objection, and I take it seriously. It also exposes the problem the chair raised: a citation that joins the PROTAC strand (Crews, Deshaies) and the glue strand (Handa) is a claim that induced proximity is one principle, and Aili's own file concedes that Ito, whose joint cereblon paper with Handa is the experimental basis, is left out and that the strands may be two achievements. I would rather see a prize with an internally consistent three-name allocation than one that is coherent only in the citation. I am glad that B060 is Aili's stated fallback, and I would ask whether Aili would put it above B046 if B014 cannot be allocated.

responses.point: Chabes puts B014 first with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, treating Ciulli's structure-guided VHL ligands as what made PROTACs a rational design discipline, and lists B060 as an alternative.
responses.response: Chabes' trio is a chain of concept, structure-guided chemistry and mechanistic rationale, and it is internally more consistent than the Handa version, since it stays within one strand. The price is that it leaves the cereblon strand, the one with approved drugs, uncredited, and Chabes says that openly. That is the same kind of cost I accept for B060, where Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan are left out. Neither of us can claim a clean allocation, so I would compare the two on maturity: B060 has a validated global clinical outcome and B014 does not yet have an approved PROTAC. I note and appreciate that Chabes lists B060 as an alternative.

responses.point: Brzezinski prefers B046 for its mechanistic basis and clean Buchwald-Hartwig allocation, while worrying about closeness to the 2010 prize and Kosugi's precursor work, and treats B014 as an alternative if its strands can be allocated within three names.
responses.response: I agree that B046 has the cleanest allocation on the table and I list it as an alternative this round. Brzezinski's own file names the unresolved difficulty: whether the committee can state in one sentence what C-N coupling adds to the 2010 prize. I see the answer as ligand-controlled reductive elimination from an amido-palladium intermediate, which is a real mechanistic step and not only a new nucleophile, but a committee that sees it as a heteroatom extension of a recognised concept will not be moved by that. On the membrane side, Brzezinski works with membrane proteins and may see LNP delivery as formulation rather than chemistry. I would ask whether the phase-behaviour principles (pKa-dependent charge, non-bilayer transitions) count as chemistry for him, as I think they do.

responses.point: Somfai argues that B046 is a conceptual advance and not only a procedure, that Kosugi's stoichiometric tin-amide chemistry is excluded on generality grounds that the Committee should state openly, and that the 2010 overlap is the main reservation.
responses.response: The generality argument for excluding Kosugi is coherent and I would accept it for B046 if it were stated in the citation. The same reasoning bears on my own case: I exclude Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan because the founding entrapment and pH-triggered release principles came first, not because their work was minor, and I must state that as openly as Somfai asks of B046. I do not agree that the conceptual step in B046 is clearly larger than its 2010 neighbour, since it keeps the same catalytic cycle. Somfai accepts that point in his case against, so the two of us differ on weight and not on facts.

responses.point: Zou calls B046 the strongest candidate when impact, originality, maturity and attribution are weighed together, and says that B014 offers a new modality that C-N coupling does not.
responses.response: Zou's criteria are the right ones and I think they need to be applied to B060 too. On maturity and attribution B060 is weaker than B046 and I accept that. On impact it has more to show, since the products are in use worldwide. On originality, Zou's own file says B014 is a new modality that B046 is not, and I would add that B060 is a self-assembled physical-chemical design solution that no earlier prize has covered. I would ask Zou whether the attribution cost of B060 outweighs this, or whether a clean two-name credit is decisive. For me it is not decisive when the two-name prize overlaps the 2010 award.

responses.point: Linke prefers B027 (Car and Parrinello) for its unambiguous two-author credit and four decades of use, while acknowledging little appetite for a third computational prize after 2013 and 2024.
responses.response: I agree that the two-author credit for B027 is the cleanest of any candidate and that the method is mature. I do not have the expertise in electronic-structure methods to judge its relative chemical weight, and I do not want to rank it on attribution alone. Linke's own concern that the Committee may not want another computational prize is a reason I put B027 outside my alternatives, although I would not oppose it as a prize if the Committee preferred it. The chair asked whether any member ranks B027 or B060 above B014 and B046: I rank B060 above both, but I would take B014 or B046 over B027 only if the third-place and Kosugi issues can be stated cleanly.

responses.point: Aqvist prefers B014 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, says that Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto, Ito and Kim have serious claims, and states that B027 is the cleaner prize if the B014 attribution cannot be defended.
responses.response: Aqvist's own file says that the attribution problem decides between B014 and B027, and I read that as an acknowledgement that B014 is not yet ready to go forward unchanged. That supports my view that an unresolved three-name cut should count against a candidate, which also applies to B060. I think the difference is that B060's cut concerns who established one chain of principles, while B014's cut concerns whether two strands are one achievement.

uncertainties: Whether the Vancouver trio is the right cut or whether Anderson, Langer or MacLachlan should displace one of them, and the early priority in the ionizable-lipid papers, which I am recalling from memory.
Whether the Committee will treat LNP delivery as a distinct chemical discovery or as formulation engineering following the 2023 Medicine prize.
Whether B014 can be given a defensible allocation across the PROTAC and cereblon strands; if it can, its novelty argument is stronger than mine.
Whether the absence of any majority means the Committee should defer to the candidate with the least contested credit rather than the candidate I judge most original.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my research field (lipid self-assembly, membrane physical chemistry, lipid-protein co-assembly) overlaps strongly with B060 and less with the phase-separation candidate B007. I have no personal, institutional or collaborative tie to any credited name on any shortlisted part that I know of. I serve with Lund colleagues Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and I regard this as no conflict for any shortlisted candidate. No member's round-1 file asks me to recuse. I disclose that I may overrate the lipid phase-behaviour side of the story, and I am not recusing.
